objective: By the end of this lesson you can describe the effects, corrective action and safety considerations of each aeromedical factor in the PTS, explain spatial disorientation and the illusions of instrument flight from the inner ear outward, demonstrate disorientation safely to a learner under the hood, and spot hypoxia, fatigue, stress and the rest in your learner and in yourself before they spoil an IFR flight.
why: Some aspect of human factors now accounts for over 80 percent of all accidents, and flying in IMC can produce sensations that mislead the body's sensory system [[23:68|IFH 3-1]]. Spatial disorientation alone was linked to nearly 200 accidents from 2008 to 2013, more than 70% of them fatal, and disoriented pilots may not know it [[24:108|AFH 5-3]]. Your instrument learners will meet these hazards in cloud and at night, often tired at the end of a long day, so they need to know the signs and the fix before they need them.

warmup: Think first: your instrument student flies a night IFR cross-country after a full workday. Two hours in, in cloud at 9,000 feet, she levels the wings after a long, shallow turn on vectors and says the airplane is now banking the other way, and you notice she was slow on the last two radio calls. Which aeromedical factors could be in play, which do you deal with first, and what would you change in the plan next time?

key_terms.def: The lack of orientation with regard to the position, attitude or movement of the airplane in space [[1:428|PHAK 17-6]].
Three fluid-filled tubes in each inner ear, at about right angles in pitch, roll and yaw, that detect angular acceleration [[23:71|IFH 3-4]].
Inner-ear organs that detect linear acceleration and gravity; forward acceleration feels like the head tilting back [[23:71|IFH 3-4]] [[23:72|IFH 3-5]].
A bank entered too slowly to be felt, then corrected abruptly, feels like a bank the other way; the pilot may roll back into it or lean in the seat [[34:185|AIM 8-1-5]].
An abrupt head movement in a prolonged constant-rate turn creates a feeling of rotation on a different axis; the AIM calls it the most overwhelming of all illusions in flight [[34:185|AIM 8-1-5]].
In a coordinated turn no longer felt, the pilot sees the altitude loss, feels a wings-level descent, pulls back and tightens the spiral [[34:185|AIM 8-1-5]].
A rapid acceleration feels like a nose-up attitude and a rapid deceleration like nose-down, especially without good visual references [[23:73|IFH 3-6]].
A state of oxygen deficiency in the body sufficient to impair functions of the brain and other organs [[34:182|AIM 8-1-2]].
The maximum time a pilot has to make and carry out rational, life-saving decisions at a given altitude without supplemental oxygen [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]].
An abnormal increase in the volume of air breathed in and out, which blows off carbon dioxide; it can start subconsciously in a stressful moment [[34:184|AIM 8-1-3]].
Symptoms from nitrogen dissolved in the body coming out of solution as bubbles when pressure drops; joint pain, the bends, is the most common [[1:440|PHAK 17-18]].
A kind of acute fatigue that disrupts timing and narrows attention to the center of vision, with loss of accuracy and smoothness [[1:435|PHAK 17-13]].

chunks.title: What the examiner asks, and the IMSAFE check for two

body.p: The PTS objective for this Task is instructional knowledge: for each of nine factors, from hypoxia to stress and fatigue, you describe the **effects**, the **corrective action** and the **safety considerations** (FAA-S-8081-9E, Area II, Task B). The PTS also asks evaluators to use scenario-based questions where possible and to emphasize your ability to teach spatial disorientation (FAA-S-8081-9E, Introduction). Expect "your student says this, what do you do?" more than "define hypoxia."

The IFH explains why this weighs more in instrument training: flying in IMC can produce sensations that mislead the body's sensory system, and a safe pilot has to understand them and counteract them [[23:68|IFH 3-1]]. The IFH leaves the physiological, psychological and medical factors to the PHAK [[23:68|IFH 3-1]], so this lesson uses PHAK Chapter 17 and AIM Chapter 8 for those. The CFI lesson AI.II.A covers the same factors from the primary instructor's seat; this lesson adds the instrument side, and FII.VI.H covers the unusual attitude recoveries that disorientation leads to.

Use one tool for both people in the airplane. The IMSAFE checklist covers illness, medication, stress, alcohol, fatigue and emotion [[25:12|AIH 1-8]]. In flight instruction the pilot risk category includes the learner and the instructor, and you have to be tuned in to your own aeromedical state as well as the learner's [[25:190|AIH 10-6]]. Monitor your own risks with IMSAFE, and build enough trust that learners tell you about their own issues well before a flight so it can be rescheduled [[25:191|AIH 10-7]]. The regulations add one hard limit for you: no more than 8 hours of flight training in any 24 consecutive hours [[60:346|14 CFR 61.195(a)]].

callout.text: How it is tested (FAA-S-8081-9E): the Area II note has the evaluator select Tasks A and D and at least one other Task, so this Task can come up for an initial CFII applicant. If you already hold a flight instructor certificate with an airplane rating, the PTS table for adding an instrument instructor rating lists Tasks A and C as the mandatory Area II Tasks. Either way, the PTS Introduction tells evaluators to emphasize your demonstrated ability to teach spatial disorientation throughout the test.

check.q: An examiner says, "Talk to me about carbon monoxide." What three things should your answer cover?
check.a: The effects, the corrective action and the safety considerations, said the way you would teach them (FAA-S-8081-9E, Area II, Task B). For CO: hypemic hypoxia and its symptoms, heater off and fresh air, and a CO detector as a safety consideration [[1:434|PHAK 17-12]] [[34:184|AIM 8-1-4]].

chunks.title: Hypoxia: the types, the altitudes that matter and the fix

body.p: **Hypoxia.** Hypoxia means not enough oxygen, and the main concern is the brain, since any reduction in mental function in flight can lead to life-threatening errors [[1:425|PHAK 17-3]]. Teach the four types by cause: hypoxic (not enough oxygen available, as with the lower partial pressure of oxygen at altitude), hypemic (the blood cannot carry enough oxygen; CO poisoning is the most common form), stagnant (oxygen-rich blood is not flowing, for example from G loads or cold) and histotoxic (the cells cannot use the oxygen, from alcohol and other drugs) [[1:425|PHAK 17-3]] [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]].

**Effects at the altitudes your learners fly.** Night vision deteriorates at a cabin altitude as low as 5,000 feet. Other significant effects usually do not occur in a normal healthy pilot below 12,000 feet; from 12,000 to 15,000 feet judgment, memory, alertness, coordination and calculation are impaired, and performance can seriously deteriorate within 15 minutes at 15,000 feet [[34:182|AIM 8-1-2]]. As hypoxia worsens, the field of vision narrows and instrument interpretation can become difficult, and the pilot can have a false sense of security [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]]. For an instrument pilot that is the worst pair: a shrinking scan and no feeling that anything is wrong.

**Higher up, and time of useful consciousness.** Above 15,000 feet cabin altitude the visual field grays to tunnel vision and the lips and fingernails turn blue (cyanosis); the ability to take corrective and protective action is lost in 20 to 30 minutes at 18,000 feet and in 5 to 12 minutes at 20,000 feet, soon followed by unconsciousness [[34:182|AIM 8-1-2]]. Time of useful consciousness is the most time a pilot has to make and carry out rational, life-saving decisions without supplemental oxygen, and it drops rapidly as altitude rises above 10,000 feet [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]]. PHAK Figure 17-1 below lists it by altitude, but its 30 minutes or more at 20,000 feet is longer than the AIM's 5 to 12 minutes [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]] [[34:182|AIM 8-1-2]]. Application: use the shorter AIM time as the planning number.

Other factors lower the altitude at which hypoxia matters. CO from exhaust or smoking, anemia and some medications cut the blood's oxygen-carrying capacity; small amounts of alcohol and drugs such as antihistamines, tranquilizers, sedatives and analgesics make the brain more susceptible; and extreme heat or cold, fever and anxiety raise the body's oxygen demand [[34:182|AIM 8-1-2]]. The IFH adds that at night oxygen deprivation causes a significant reduction in vision, and returning to a lower altitude does not restore it as quickly as it was lost [[23:69|IFH 3-2]].

**Corrective action.** Treatment is a lower altitude, supplemental oxygen, or both [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]]. Prevention is heeding the factors that reduce tolerance, using oxygen and keeping a comfortable cabin altitude; for best protection the AIM encourages oxygen above 10,000 feet by day and above 5,000 feet at night [[34:183|AIM 8-1-2]]. Hypoxia is hard to recognize when it comes on gradually, and an altitude chamber flight helps a pilot learn the signs [[34:183|AIM 8-1-2]].

callout.text: 14 CFR 91.211(a): at cabin pressure altitudes above 12,500 feet up to and including 14,000 feet, the required minimum flight crew must use oxygen for the part of the flight at those altitudes that lasts more than 30 minutes; above 14,000 feet, for the entire time; above 15,000 feet, each occupant must be provided with oxygen [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211(a)]].

Application: on a night IFR trip with a 9,000-foot MEA, the rule requires nothing, but the AIM recommendation for night does [[34:183|AIM 8-1-2]]. Make it a personal-minimums question and let the learner decide out loud.

check.q: Climbing to 11,000 feet IFR at night without oxygen, your learner says she feels great, almost cheerful. What do you teach from that?
check.a: Euphoria can be an early symptom, and hypoxia can give a false sense of security [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]]. The AIM recommends oxygen above 5,000 feet at night for best protection [[34:183|AIM 8-1-2]].

body.p: **Hyperventilation.** It is an abnormal increase in the volume of air breathed in and out, and it can start subconsciously when a stressful situation comes up in flight. It blows off carbon dioxide and brings lightheadedness, a feeling of suffocation, drowsiness, tingling in the extremities and coolness; the pilot may react with even more rapid breathing, and incoordination, disorientation, painful muscle spasms and finally unconsciousness can follow [[34:184|AIM 8-1-3]]. It happens more often among pilots than is generally recognized and seldom incapacitates completely, but the symptoms alarm an uninformed pilot [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]].

An unexpected stressful situation can raise the breathing rate without the pilot noticing, and pilots at higher altitudes tend to breathe faster than normal, with or without oxygen [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]]. Application: the first flight in real cloud, the first partial panel approach and the checkride are the moments to watch.

**Corrective action.** Breathing normally is both the best prevention and the best cure. Slowing the breathing rate, breathing into a paper bag or talking aloud helps, and recovery is usually rapid [[1:427|PHAK 17-5]]. The symptoms subside within a few minutes once the rate and depth of breathing are consciously brought back under control [[34:184|AIM 8-1-3]].

callout.text: Hypoxia or hyperventilation? The early symptoms are similar, and both can happen at once. If on oxygen, set the regulator to 100 percent and check that the system is working first, then work on the breathing [[34:184|AIM 8-1-3]].

Application: ask a tense learner to talk you through the approach. Talking aloud helps overcome hyperventilation [[1:427|PHAK 17-5]], and like the learner-tells step of the demonstration method it lets you hear what the learner is thinking [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

check.q: On her first approach in actual IMC, at 3,000 feet and not on oxygen, your learner reports tingling fingers and lightheadedness. What is the likely cause?
check.a: Hyperventilation from stress [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]]; significant altitude hypoxia effects usually do not occur below 12,000 feet [[34:182|AIM 8-1-2]]. Have her slow her breathing and talk aloud [[1:427|PHAK 17-5]].

chunks.title: Gas in the body: ears, sinuses and scuba nitrogen

body.p: **Middle ear and sinus problems.** In a climb, expanding air in the middle ear pushes the Eustachian tube open and escapes on its own. In a descent the pilot must open the tube by swallowing, yawning or tensing the throat muscles, or, if those do not work, with the Valsalva maneuver: close the mouth, pinch the nose and try to blow through the nostrils [[34:183|AIM 8-1-2]]. A cold, sore throat or nasal allergy can block it. An ear block brings severe ear pain and hearing loss that can last from hours to days, and the eardrum can rupture in flight or after landing [[34:183|AIM 8-1-2]].

A sinus block happens most often during descent: excruciating pain above the eyebrows or in the upper cheeks, aching upper teeth and sometimes bloody mucus [[34:183|AIM 8-1-2]]. Slow descent rates can reduce the pain [[1:427|PHAK 17-5]]. Prevention is not flying with an upper respiratory infection or nasal allergy: decongestant sprays and drops usually do not protect adequately, oral decongestants have side effects that can impair performance, and a block that does not clear shortly after landing needs a physician [[34:183|AIM 8-1-2]] [[34:184|AIM 8-1-2]].

callout.text: Application: an IFR lesson is a string of descents: arrival, step-downs and several approaches. A learner with a cold gets a ground lesson. If a block starts in flight anyway, ask ATC for a slower descent or more time before the approach rather than pressing on.

body.p: **Evolved gases from scuba diving.** Diving loads the body with extra nitrogen. Flying too soon lets it come out of solution at the lower cabin pressure, causing altitude decompression sickness and a serious in-flight emergency [[34:184|AIM 8-1-2]]. The most common symptom is joint pain, the bends [[1:440|PHAK 17-18]]; PHAK Figure 17-10 also lists brain and nerve signs (confusion, headache, vision changes, tingling), the chokes (burning chest pain, shortness of breath, dry cough) and skin itching or mottling, and bends pain can come at altitude, in the descent or many hours later [[1:441|PHAK 17-19]]. Wait at least 12 hours before flying up to 8,000 feet after a dive that needed no decompression stops, at least 24 hours after a dive that needed a controlled ascent, and at least 24 hours after any dive before flying above 8,000 feet. These are actual MSL altitudes, not cabin altitudes, to allow for a decompression in flight [[34:184|AIM 8-1-2]].

Corrective action for DCS: oxygen mask on with the regulator at 100 percent, an emergency descent and a landing as soon as possible, a painful joint kept still, and medical help from an FAA medical officer, AME, military flight surgeon or hyperbaric specialist even if the symptoms go away. Symptoms can also start after landing [[1:440|PHAK 17-18]].

callout.text: 12, 24, 24: twelve hours up to 8,000 feet after a no-decompression dive, twenty-four after a decompression dive, twenty-four after any dive above 8,000 feet MSL [[34:184|AIM 8-1-2]]. Application: check the planned IFR altitude and the MEAs before you quote 12 hours.

check.q: Your learner surfaced from a no-decompression dive at 0900 and wants to fly an IFR trip at 9,000 feet MSL in a pressurized airplane at 1600. What do you say?
check.a: Not today. Above 8,000 feet the wait is at least 24 hours after any dive, and the altitudes are actual MSL, not cabin altitudes [[34:184|AIM 8-1-2]].

chunks.title: How the body senses orientation, and why IMC fools it

body.p: **Spatial disorientation** is the lack of orientation with regard to the position, attitude or movement of the airplane in space [[1:428|PHAK 17-6]]. Orientation comes from three systems: visual, vestibular (the inner ear) and postural (nerves in the skin, joints and muscles) [[23:69|IFH 3-2]]. In VMC the eyes usually win over false sensations; take the visual cues away, as IMC does, and false sensations can disorient a pilot quickly [[23:70|IFH 3-3]].

The semicircular canals sense angular acceleration and the otolith organs sense linear acceleration and gravity. Because of friction, the fluid in a canal may take about 15 to 20 seconds to reach the canal's speed [[23:71|IFH 3-4]]. A rotational acceleration of 2 degrees per second or lower is below the canals' detection threshold [[1:429|PHAK 17-7]]. In a prolonged, constant turn the fluid catches up and the brain gets the false impression that turning has stopped; rolling level then feels like a turn the other way [[23:72|IFH 3-5]].

The otoliths cannot tell acceleration from a head tilt: forward acceleration feels like the head tilting back, so during takeoff and acceleration a pilot may sense a steeper climb and tend to push the nose down [[23:72|IFH 3-5]]. The postural system has the same weakness, since the body cannot tell gravity from the forces of maneuvering [[1:428|PHAK 17-6]], and skids and slips feel like banking or tilting [[23:72|IFH 3-5]]. Fatigue or illness can make these sensations worse and lead to subtle incapacitation [[23:72|IFH 3-5]].

callout.text: Canals: rotation. Otoliths: acceleration and gravity. Seat of the pants: fooled by both. In IMC the only reliable sense is the eyes, on the instruments [[23:70|IFH 3-3]].

check.q: A learner asks why she never felt the airplane roll into a 20° bank while she copied a clearance. What do you answer?
check.a: A slow roll can stay below the canals' detection threshold, a rotational acceleration of 2 degrees per second or lower [[1:429|PHAK 17-7]], and once a turn is steady the fluid catches up so the turn is no longer felt [[23:72|IFH 3-5]].

chunks.title: Vestibular illusions you will meet in IMC

body.p: The vestibular system is responsible for most of the illusions that lead to spatial disorientation [[23:72|IFH 3-5]]. Teach each one with the IMC situation where it shows up, what the disoriented pilot does, and the instrument habit that stops it.

body.p: Where they show up in instrument training (application): a long turn on vectors while the learner looks for a chart sets up the leans and Coriolis; the full-power missed approach in cloud is a rapid acceleration, the IMC cousin of the takeoff case the IFH describes [[23:73|IFH 3-6]]; and convective turbulence brings the elevator illusion.

callout.text: Every vestibular illusion makes the wrong control input feel right. The fix is the same each time: trust the instruments and disregard the sensory perceptions [[23:76|IFH 3-9]].

check.q: On a missed approach in cloud your learner adds full power, then lets the nose sink well below the climb attitude. What illusion fits and what do you teach?
check.a: The somatogravic illusion: rapid acceleration feels like a nose-up attitude, so the pilot pushes over [[23:73|IFH 3-6]]. Hold the climb attitude on the attitude indicator and disregard the feeling [[23:76|IFH 3-9]].

chunks.title: Visual illusions, from cloud tops to the runway at minimums

body.p: Two illusions that lead to spatial disorientation involve only the visual system [[23:74|IFH 3-7]]. **False horizon:** a sloping cloud formation, an obscured horizon, an aurora, a dark scene spread with ground lights and stars, or geometric patterns of ground lights can give the wrong horizon, and the pilot may put the airplane in a dangerous attitude [[23:74|IFH 3-7]]. **Autokinesis:** in the dark a stationary light appears to move when stared at for many seconds, and a pilot who tries to align with it can lose control [[23:74|IFH 3-7]]. Application: on top of a sloping layer, or in and out of cloud at night, the attitude indicator is the horizon.

An instrument approach ends with a switch from the instruments to visual cues for landing, so the landing illusions belong in instrument training [[23:76|IFH 3-9]]. A narrower-than-usual or upsloping runway, featureless terrain, rain on the windscreen and haze all make the pilot feel higher or farther away than he is and fly a lower approach; bright runway lights with few lights around them make the runway seem closer and lead to a higher approach; and flying into fog feels like pitching up, so the pilot steepens the approach, often quite abruptly [[34:185|AIM 8-1-5]] [[34:186|AIM 8-1-5]].

bullets: Anticipate illusions at unfamiliar airports, especially at night or in bad weather, and check the airport diagram and Chart Supplement for slope, terrain and lighting [[1:432|PHAK 17-10]] [[1:433|PHAK 17-11]].
Keep the altimeter in the scan on every approach, day and night [[1:433|PHAK 17-11]].
Use the electronic glideslope, VASI or PAPI, and the visual descent point found on many nonprecision charts [[1:433|PHAK 17-11]].
Expect a higher chance of an approach accident when an emergency or other activity distracts from usual procedures [[1:434|PHAK 17-12]].
At night, whenever position relative to the runway or altitude is in doubt, go around [[24:222|AFH 11-5]].

check.q: Breaking out at minimums in heavy rain, your learner feels high and starts to duck under the glideslope. What is happening and what do you say?
check.a: Rain on the windscreen gives an illusion of greater height, which leads to a lower approach [[34:186|AIM 8-1-5]]. Stay on the glideslope and keep the altimeter in the scan [[1:433|PHAK 17-11]].

body.p: Disorientation from these illusions can be prevented only by visual reference to reliable, fixed points on the ground or to the flight instruments [[34:185|AIM 8-1-5]]. In IMC that leaves the instruments. The IFH method: recognize the problem, disregard the false sensations, rely on the flight instruments and use the eyes to determine the attitude [[23:70|IFH 3-3]].

The AFH names three ways it plays out. **Recognized:** the pilot sees the upset developing and corrects it. **Unrecognized:** the pilot does not know an upset is developing and takes no action. **Incapacitating:** the pilot cannot recover, from not understanding events, lacking the skill, or being overwhelmed [[24:108|AFH 5-3]]. Disoriented pilots may not know they are wrong, and some see the conflict between their senses and the instruments but let the airplane drift because they cannot resolve it [[24:108|AFH 5-3]]. Training aims to keep learners in the first group.

bullets: A cross-check with minimal head movement, and dropped items retrieved slowly [[23:73|IFH 3-6]].

Small, smooth corrections. Large corrections with rapid attitude changes may lead to spatial disorientation [[23:155|IFH 6-22]], and abrupt reactions to altitude errors set up an oscillation that can disorient the pilot and fix the eyes on the altimeter [[23:197|IFH 7-36]].
The ball centered: slipping and skidding sensations can aggravate disorientation and slow a recovery [[23:189|IFH 7-28]].

Anything unusual on the panel: assume an unusual attitude and speed up the cross-check [[23:188|IFH 7-27]]. Nose-low and turning, as above: reduce power, level the wings by the turn coordinator with coordinated aileron and rudder, then raise the nose; the instinctive reaction is to pull [[23:189|IFH 7-28]].
Never try to recover by sensations other than sight; the IFH lists it as a common error [[23:190|IFH 7-29]].

callout.text: Application: give the learner a spoken trigger, such as "my body says left turn, the attitude indicator says level, I fly the attitude indicator." It turns the conflict the AFH describes into a decision.

check.q: In cloud your learner says, "I know the attitude indicator shows level, but we are turning left." What do you do?
check.a: Name it as a sensation that conflicts with the instruments, have her hold the wings level on the attitude indicator, confirm with the turn coordinator and heading, and disregard the feeling [[23:70|IFH 3-3]]. Pilots who cannot resolve that conflict let the airplane drift [[24:108|AFH 5-3]].

chunks.title: Demonstrating disorientation safely under the hood

body.p: The demonstrations teach how susceptible the body is, that attitude judged by feel is often false, how head movement adds to it, and why to trust the instruments [[23:74|IFH 3-7]]. Any false sensation is an effective demonstration, and feeling nothing is one too, since it shows the body cannot detect bank or roll [[23:74|IFH 3-7]]. The IFH sample syllabus puts a spatial disorientation demonstration in Lesson 3, alongside human factors ground training [[23:342|IFH B-1]].

body.p: A learner-flown version works too: eyes closed and head tilted, the learner follows your control instructions until disoriented, then you say to look up and recover [[23:75|IFH 3-8]]. Brief the sensations before you fly them, as the AIH asks for stalls, so the learner knows what to expect and how to react [[25:45|AIH 2-12]]. Be honest about one limit: when the learner is told to close the eyes, the surprise disappears [[24:107|AFH 5-2]], while a real upset brings startle, which scenario-based training with realistic distractions helps prepare for [[24:108|AFH 5-3]].

callout.text: Safety considerations: never at low altitudes and never without an instructor or appropriate safety pilot [[23:75|IFH 3-8]]. Brief and use the three-step exchange of flight controls with a visual check [[25:178|AIH 9-8]] [[25:179|AIH 9-9]]. Rough air, abrupt maneuvers and tension make airsickness more likely [[25:46|AIH 2-13]], so start gentle, save the head-movement roll for last, and stop at the first sign of sickness. Application: while the learner's eyes are closed you are the only lookout.

Application: with the view-limiting device on, have the learner close the eyes as well, then open them to the instruments, not out the window, to recover. The habit you are building is "when the body lies, look at the panel." Recovery from unusual attitudes is taught in FII.VI.H.

check.q: Your learner felt nothing during the climbing-while-turning demonstration and says it did not work. What do you tell her?
check.a: Feeling nothing is still an effective demonstration: it shows the body cannot detect bank or roll [[23:74|IFH 3-7]].

body.p: **Motion sickness** comes from the brain getting conflicting messages about the state of the body. Symptoms are general discomfort, nausea, dizziness, paleness, sweating and vomiting [[1:434|PHAK 17-12]]. It often appears on early flights and usually goes away within the first few lessons; anxiety and stress contribute, and it is no reflection on the learner's ability as a pilot [[1:434|PHAK 17-12]].

Instrument training has its own triggers (application): hood work takes away the outside view, unusual attitude recoveries and disorientation demonstrations are abrupt, and cloud often means rough air. The AIH confirms that rough air, unexpected abrupt maneuvers, tension and apprehension all add to airsickness [[25:46|AIH 2-13]].

bullets: End the instructional flight as soon as early sickness appears; as resistance builds, flights can be lengthened [[25:46|AIH 2-13]].
Keep the learner busy on the controls: learners are much less apt to get sick while flying the airplane themselves [[25:46|AIH 2-13]].
Fresh air vents, focusing on objects outside the airplane and avoiding unnecessary head movement may help [[1:434|PHAK 17-12]].
For a learner prone to it, avoid turbulent days and start with shorter flights [[1:434|PHAK 17-12]].

callout.text: Medications like Dramamine can prevent airsickness in passengers but are not recommended while flying because they can cause drowsiness [[1:434|PHAK 17-12]]. Motion sickness agents are on the AIM list of drugs whose side effects can impair judgment, alertness and coordination [[34:180|AIM 8-1-1]].

Application: when a learner gets queasy under the hood, take the hood off, give an outside reference and fresh air, and let the learner fly gently home. Debrief it as normal so the next hood lesson does not start with dread.

check.q: A learner prone to airsickness asks whether to take a motion sickness pill before the next unusual attitude lesson. What do you say?
check.a: No: such medicines can cause drowsiness and are not recommended while flying [[1:434|PHAK 17-12]]. Use shorter flights, smooth air, fresh air and the learner on the controls instead [[25:46|AIH 2-13]].

chunks.title: Alcohol and drugs: the rule, and what they do in cloud

body.p: **Alcohol and drugs.** 14 CFR 91.17(a) bars acting or attempting to act as a crewmember within 8 hours after drinking any alcoholic beverage, while under the influence of alcohol, while using any drug that affects the faculties in any way contrary to safety, or with an alcohol concentration of 0.04 or greater [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17(a)]]. The RMH teaches it as three limits, time, quantity and performance, and warns that aftereffects such as hangover can last beyond 8 hours [[30:23|RMH 3-5]]. The AIM's rule of thumb is 12 to 24 hours from bottle to throttle, depending on the amount, since nothing speeds up the destruction of alcohol [[34:181|AIM 8-1-1]].

Why it matters more in cloud: alcohol makes a pilot much more susceptible to disorientation and hypoxia [[34:181|AIM 8-1-1]], and the PHAK lists inner-ear disturbance and spatial disorientation for up to 48 hours among its effects [[1:439|PHAK 17-17]]. Altitude multiplies alcohol's effect on the brain, so two drinks may act like three or four, and a hangover still counts as being under the influence [[1:437|PHAK 17-15]].

Drugs: tranquilizers, sedatives, strong pain relievers and cough suppressants can impair judgment, memory, alertness, coordination, vision and calculation directly; antihistamines, blood pressure drugs, muscle relaxants and agents for diarrhea and motion sickness can do it as side effects; and any medication that depresses the nervous system makes a pilot much more susceptible to hypoxia [[34:180|AIM 8-1-1]]. Diphenhydramine causes drowsiness and stays in the system a long time [[1:438|PHAK 17-16]]. The FAA states that marijuana is an illicit drug under federal law and its use by airmen is prohibited [[1:439|PHAK 17-17]].

head: Rule or guideline
What it says
rows: If you hold a medical certificate: no acting as PIC or required pilot crewmember while you know or have reason to know of a condition, or take medication or treatment, that leaves you unable to meet that certificate's requirements [[60:233|14 CFR 61.53(a)]]. For operations that need no medical certificate (61.23(b)), and for 61.23(c) operations by a U.S. driver's license holder, the test is any condition that would make you unable to operate the aircraft safely [[60:233|14 CFR 61.53(b)]] [[60:233|14 CFR 61.53(c)]]
Except in an emergency, no carrying a person who appears intoxicated or under the influence of drugs, except a medical patient under proper care [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17(b)]]
New medicine (PHAK)
Wait at least 48 hours after the first dose to see whether it has side effects [[1:440|PHAK 17-18]]
Medicine with side effects such as sedation (PHAK)
Wait at least five maximal dosing intervals; a 5 to 6 hour interval means 30 hours [[1:440|PHAK 17-18]]
Safest rule (AIM)
Do not fly as a crewmember while taking any medication unless approved by the FAA [[34:180|AIM 8-1-1]]; in doubt, ask an AME [[1:440|PHAK 17-18]]

callout.text: Application: make medication an IMSAFE question at every preflight, not only when a learner looks unwell. Cold medicine taken the night before is the common catch.

check.q: Your instrument student's dinner with two glasses of wine ended 10 hours before an IFR lesson, so she meets the 8-hour rule. What else do you weigh?
check.a: Eight hours is only the time limit; she also may not be under the influence or at 0.04 or more [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17(a)]]. The AIM suggests 12 to 24 hours, and alcohol raises susceptibility to disorientation and hypoxia [[34:181|AIM 8-1-1]].

chunks.title: Carbon monoxide on a winter IFR flight

body.p: **Carbon monoxide poisoning.** CO is a colorless, odorless and tasteless gas in exhaust fumes, and even small amounts breathed over time significantly reduce the blood's ability to carry oxygen [[34:184|AIM 8-1-4]]. It attaches to hemoglobin about 200 times more easily than oxygen, causing hypemic hypoxia, and the body needs up to 48 hours to get rid of it [[1:434|PHAK 17-12]]. Most light-airplane heaters work by air flowing over the exhaust manifold, so exhaust escaping through cracks and seals reaches the cabin; this causes several nonfatal and fatal accidents every year [[34:184|AIM 8-1-4]].

Effects: headache, blurred vision, dizziness, drowsiness and loss of muscle power [[1:434|PHAK 17-12]]. CO also lowers the altitude at which hypoxia becomes significant [[34:182|AIM 8-1-2]] and impairs dark adaptation [[34:186|AIM 8-1-6]], so a night IFR flight with the heater on stacks several hazards. Smoking alone can raise CO in the blood to effects like those of flying at 8,000 feet [[1:434|PHAK 17-12]].

callout.text: Corrective action: smell exhaust, or feel headache, drowsiness or dizziness with the heater on, and suspect CO. Shut off the heater, open the air vents and windows, use oxygen if available, and get medical treatment if symptoms are severe or continue after landing [[34:184|AIM 8-1-4]] [[1:434|PHAK 17-12]]. CO can be dangerous with no exhaust smell at all; inexpensive detectors are widely available [[1:434|PHAK 17-12]].

Application: you and the learner breathe the same air. If the learner reports symptoms, check yourself, take a bigger share of the flying and decisions, and tell ATC early so a nearby landing is easy to get.

check.q: Climbing out on a cold night IFR departure, you both get headaches and your learner keeps yawning. What first?
check.a: Suspect CO: heater off, vents and windows open, oxygen if available, and medical treatment if symptoms are severe or continue after landing [[34:184|AIM 8-1-4]] [[1:434|PHAK 17-12]].

chunks.title: Stress and fatigue: night, IMC and the long day

body.p: **Stress** is the body's response to physical and psychological demands; hormones such as adrenaline raise heart rate, breathing, blood pressure and sweating [[1:434|PHAK 17-12]]. Acute stress is an immediate perceived threat. Chronic stress exceeds the ability to cope, performance falls off rapidly, and a pilot in that state should not fly and should see a physician [[1:434|PHAK 17-12]]. Stress can distract enough to cause unwarranted risks, such as flying into deteriorating weather to keep on schedule, and stress with fatigue is an extremely hazardous combination [[34:181|AIM 8-1-1]].

**Fatigue** is one of the most treacherous hazards because it may not be apparent until serious errors are made. Acute fatigue follows strain, immobility, heavy mental workload, emotional pressure, monotony or lack of sleep; chronic fatigue comes when there is not enough recovery between episodes and needs a prolonged rest [[34:181|AIM 8-1-1]]; the PHAK adds that it is not relieved by diet, rest and sleep alone and usually needs treatment by a physician [[1:435|PHAK 17-13]]. Skill fatigue disrupts timing and narrows attention to the center of vision [[1:435|PHAK 17-13]]: on the panel, that is a shrinking cross-check.
Why **stress and fatigue** go with night and IMC:

bullets: Sleep-deprived pilots may feel fine through preflight and departure; sleepiness tends to show once established on altitude and heading, and fatigue moves from errors of omission to errors of commission to microsleeps [[25:18|AIH 1-14]].

Late night, fatigue and sustained flight above 5,000 feet can make pilots less critical and more accepting, with the guard lowest at the critical moment, such as a night instrument approach in weather after a 4-hour flight [[25:21|AIH 1-17]].

Illness, medication, alcohol, fatigue, sleep loss and mild hypoxia raise susceptibility to spatial disorientation [[23:75|IFH 3-8]] [[23:76|IFH 3-9]], and fatigue can be intensified by hypoxia [[30:23|RMH 3-5]].
The AFH's example of task saturation is a fatigued pilot who enters IMC at night and then loses the vacuum pump [[24:108|AFH 5-3]].

callout.text: Corrective action: if suffering from acute fatigue, stay on the ground; in the flight deck no training or experience overcomes it, and adequate rest is the only prevention [[1:435|PHAK 17-13]]. With more difficulties than usual, consider delaying the flight [[34:181|AIM 8-1-1]]. On flights longer than 2 hours, run the 5P check every hour [[25:21|AIH 1-17]]. The RMH lists stress and fatigue among the conditions that call for raising baseline personal minimums [[30:17|RMH 2-5]].

check.q: Your learner flew well for the first hour of a night IFR trip, but now misses a frequency change and lets the altitude drift 150 feet. She says she feels fine. What is your read?
check.a: Likely fatigue: sleepiness often shows once established on altitude and heading [[25:18|AIH 1-14]], and signs like neglected secondary tasks and lost accuracy show to others before the pilot notices [[25:46|AIH 2-13]] [[25:47|AIH 2-14]].

body.p: During flight instruction you are normally the only one who sees the learner under pressure [[25:48|AIH 2-15]]. Keep a watch list and say out loud what you see and what you do about it. That is also how you answer the examiner.

head: What you notice
What it may be
What you do
rows: Euphoria, headache, drowsiness, slow reactions at altitude [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]]
Hypoxia
Descend, use oxygen, or both [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]]
Fast breathing, tingling, lightheadedness when tense [[34:184|AIM 8-1-3]]
Hyperventilation; if on oxygen, check it first [[34:184|AIM 8-1-3]]
Slow the breathing; have the learner talk aloud [[1:427|PHAK 17-5]]
Leaning in the seat after a roll-out, or control inputs that fight the attitude indicator
The leans or another illusion [[34:185|AIM 8-1-5]]
Name it, point to the attitude indicator, and take the controls if needed [[25:179|AIH 9-9]]
Stop and stare at one instrument when something looks wrong
Slow cross-check and fixation [[23:189|IFH 7-28]]
Prompt the full cross-check; practice until recognition is immediate [[23:189|IFH 7-28]]
Pale, sweating, nauseated [[1:434|PHAK 17-12]]
Motion sickness
Fresh air, learner on the controls, end the flight [[25:46|AIH 2-13]]
Inattention, errors in timing, neglected secondary tasks, lost accuracy, no awareness of errors piling up, irritability [[25:47|AIH 2-14]]
Acute fatigue
A break, or end the lesson; fatigue sets lesson length [[25:46|AIH 2-13]]
Extreme over-cooperation, inappropriate laughter, very rapid mood changes, anger at you [[25:48|AIH 2-15]]
Abnormal reaction to stress
Careful evaluation; no single sign is proof [[25:48|AIH 2-15]]

body.p: Then turn the list on yourself. Flight instruction requires you to watch your own aeromedical state as well as the learner's [[25:190|AIH 10-6]], and 8 hours of flight training in 24 consecutive hours is the legal ceiling [[60:346|14 CFR 61.195(a)]]. All pilots are susceptible to false sensations at night and in certain weather [[24:108|AFH 5-3]], and that includes the instructor in the right seat. Never let a lesson exceed your own ability to perceive a problem, decide and physically react [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].

callout.text: Application: on a long instructing day, put the hardest IFR lesson (partial panel approaches, actual IMC, night) where you are freshest, and write your own personal minimums for instructing at night and in cloud.

check.q: It is your third lesson of the day and you have given 6.5 hours of dual. The next learner wants a 2-hour night IMC flight. What limits apply?
check.a: No more than 8 hours of flight training in 24 consecutive hours, so you have 1.5 hours left [[60:346|14 CFR 61.195(a)]], and your own IMSAFE check comes first [[25:191|AIH 10-7]].

scenario.title: Night IFR cross-country after a long day
scenario.setup: You are a new CFII. Your instrument student, a commercial pilot, is due for her long IFR cross-country in the school's single-engine airplane: six-pack panel, one vacuum pump, a cabin heater that warms air over the exhaust, and no CO detector. It is a cold winter evening. She worked a 10-hour day, has a stuffy nose, and took a nighttime cold medicine with diphenhydramine last night. The route has a 9,000-foot MEA, and the destination needs an ILS with a 500-foot ceiling in rain.

questions.q: Before you go, what do you weigh?
questions.a: Her stuffy nose and the many descents: do not fly with an upper respiratory infection, and sprays and oral decongestants are not the fix [[34:183|AIM 8-1-2]]. Diphenhydramine causes drowsiness and stays in the system a long time [[1:438|PHAK 17-16]]. After a full workday, her guard will be lowest at the night approach in weather [[25:21|AIH 1-17]], and with acute fatigue the advice is to stay on the ground [[1:435|PHAK 17-13]]. Move the flight to another day.

questions.q: A week later she is healthy and rested. At 9,000 feet for 90 minutes at night, is oxygen required, and what do you recommend?
questions.a: Not required: the crew rule starts above 12,500 feet cabin altitude [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211(a)]]. But night vision deteriorates from 5,000 feet, and the AIM encourages oxygen above 5,000 feet at night [[34:182|AIM 8-1-2]] [[34:183|AIM 8-1-2]]. Use it if the airplane has it, and have her include it in her personal minimums.

questions.q: Level in cloud with the heater on, she says she has a headache and feels drowsy. What do you do?
questions.a: Suspect CO: shut off the heater, open the vents, use oxygen if available, and get medical treatment if symptoms are severe or continue after landing [[34:184|AIM 8-1-4]] [[1:434|PHAK 17-12]]. Check yourself too: you breathe the same air.

questions.q: On vectors, in a long left turn, she drops her pencil and ducks her head to find it. What do you say?
questions.a: Stop her. A head movement in a prolonged constant-rate turn can set off the Coriolis illusion [[34:185|AIM 8-1-5]]. Fly the turn on the instruments, get the pencil later, and retrieve it with minimal head movement [[23:73|IFH 3-6]].

questions.q: At minimums in rain she sees the approach lights, feels high and starts to push below the glideslope. What is happening?
questions.a: Rain on the windscreen creates an illusion of greater height, and a pilot who does not recognize it flies a lower approach [[34:186|AIM 8-1-5]]. Hold the glideslope and keep the altimeter in the scan [[1:433|PHAK 17-11]].

questions.q: In the debrief, how do you check that she can manage these risks without you?
questions.a: Have her run IMSAFE on the flight [[25:12|AIH 1-8]] and the 5P check at each decision point, including the descent and final approach fix [[25:21|AIH 1-17]], and say what she would change. Then ask her to tell you about any aeromedical issue well before future flights, so they can be rescheduled [[25:191|AIH 10-7]].

skills.do: Explain spatial disorientation and the illusions of instrument flight to a learner, then brief, fly and debrief the disorientation demonstrations, using a positive exchange of controls and linking each sensation to an IMC situation.
skills.practice: Rehearse the brief aloud with another applicant using the IFH demonstrations [[23:75|IFH 3-8]], fly them together at a safe altitude with one of you as instructor or safety pilot [[23:75|IFH 3-8]], and use the three-step exchange every time [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

skills.do: For any of the nine factors, describe the effects, the corrective action and the safety considerations, and say how you would spot it in a learner and in yourself.
skills.practice: Make a one-page card per factor and have another applicant read you scenarios; answer in the PTS order: effect, fix, safety (FAA-S-8081-9E). Use the AIH fatigue and stress signs [[25:47|AIH 2-14]] [[25:48|AIH 2-15]] for the spot-it part.

quiz.q: Climbing to 11,000 feet at night without oxygen, your instrument student says she feels cheerful and sharp. What do you teach from that?
options: Feeling fine shows that she adapts well to the altitude
Hypoxia never affects a healthy pilot below 15,000 feet
Euphoria can be an early sign, with a false sense of security
Cheerfulness rules hypoxia out, since it starts with a headache
quiz.why: The first symptoms of hypoxia can include euphoria and a carefree feeling, and hypoxia can deceive a pilot into believing everything is normal [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]]. Night vision already deteriorates from 5,000 feet [[34:182|AIM 8-1-2]], so 15,000 feet is not a safe floor.

quiz.q: Your learner will cruise at a cabin altitude of 13,500 feet for 50 minutes. What does 14 CFR 91.211 require of the required flight crew?
options: Oxygen for the 20 minutes beyond the first 30
Oxygen for all 50 minutes at that altitude
No oxygen, since the flight stays under 14,000 feet
Oxygen only when a passenger is also on board
quiz.why: Above 12,500 feet up to 14,000 feet, the crew must use oxygen for the part of the flight at those altitudes that lasts more than 30 minutes [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211(a)]]. The whole-time rule starts above 14,000 feet, and the passenger rule above 15,000 feet.

quiz.q: On her first approach in actual IMC, at 3,000 feet and not on oxygen, your learner reports tingling fingers and lightheadedness. What is your first response?
options: Descend at once to treat the altitude hypoxia
Have her breathe faster to get more oxygen
Wait, since the symptoms always pass on their own
Have her slow her breathing and talk you through the approach
quiz.why: Stress can bring on hyperventilation; slowing the breathing and talking aloud help, and recovery is usually rapid [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]] [[1:427|PHAK 17-5]]. Significant altitude hypoxia effects usually do not occur below 12,000 feet [[34:182|AIM 8-1-2]], and faster breathing makes hyperventilation worse [[34:184|AIM 8-1-3]].

quiz.q: Your student, on oxygen at 16,000 feet, reports lightheadedness and tingling. Per the AIM, what comes first?
options: Slow the breathing, then check the oxygen later
Regulator to 100 percent; check the system
Remove the mask, since oxygen causes these symptoms
Breathe into a paper bag held over the mask
quiz.why: The early symptoms of hypoxia and hyperventilation are similar and can occur together, so on oxygen the AIM says to set 100 percent and check the system before attending to the breathing [[34:184|AIM 8-1-3]]. Slowing the breathing first would be right only if hypoxia were ruled out.

quiz.q: Your learner has a head cold and wants to fly an IFR lesson with three approaches, using a nasal spray. What does the AIM say?
options: Fly, since the spray will keep the tubes open
Fly, but use an oral decongestant instead of the spray
Do not fly with it; sprays usually do not protect
Fly, and clear the ears with a Valsalva in the climbs
quiz.why: Ear and sinus blocks are prevented by not flying with an upper respiratory infection; sprays and drops usually do not give adequate protection, and oral decongestants have side effects that can impair performance [[34:183|AIM 8-1-2]]. In a climb the air escapes on its own; descent is when the tube must be opened [[34:183|AIM 8-1-2]].

quiz.q: A student surfaced at 0800 from a dive that needed decompression stops. The IFR flight will cruise at 6,000 feet MSL. What is the earliest departure the AIM supports?
options: 1400 the same day
2000 the same day
Any time, below 8,000 feet
0800 the next day
quiz.why: After a dive that required a controlled ascent, wait at least 24 hours even for flight up to 8,000 feet [[34:184|AIM 8-1-2]]. The 12-hour wait applies only to dives without decompression stops.

quiz.q: Your learner levels the wings after a long, shallow turn in cloud and insists the airplane is now banking the other way. What explains it?
options: The turn was too gradual to feel, so leveling felt like a bank
The attitude indicator precessed and now shows a false bank
Her otolith organs read the deceleration as a bank
She stared at the heading indicator and lost the horizon
quiz.why: Rotational acceleration of 2 degrees per second or lower is below the canals' threshold, and leveling the wings after such a turn can feel like a bank the other way: the leans [[1:429|PHAK 17-7]] [[34:185|AIM 8-1-5]]. The otoliths sense linear acceleration, not roll [[23:71|IFH 3-4]].

quiz.q: In a prolonged standard-rate turn in IMC, which action by your learner is most likely to bring on the Coriolis illusion?
options: Rolling out slowly on the assigned heading
Turning her head down and aside to pick up a chart
Holding a constant bank angle on the attitude indicator the whole time
Reducing power a little to stay at altitude
quiz.why: A head movement in a different plane during a prolonged turn can set the fluid moving and create an illusion of rotation on another axis [[23:73|IFH 3-6]]. The AIM says it is prevented by avoiding sudden, extreme head movements in prolonged constant-rate turns under IFR [[34:185|AIM 8-1-5]].

quiz.q: On the missed approach in cloud your learner adds full power and lowers the nose below the climb attitude, saying the climb felt too steep. What do you name and teach?
options: Inversion illusion; level off more abruptly
Elevator illusion; reduce power until it passes
Autokinesis; stop staring at one instrument
Somatogravic; hold the climb attitude
quiz.why: Rapid acceleration stimulates the otolith organs like a head tilt back, creating an illusion of nose-up, and the disoriented pilot pushes nose-low [[23:73|IFH 3-6]]. The inversion illusion comes from an abrupt level-off, not a power increase [[23:73|IFH 3-6]].

quiz.q: Disoriented in cloud, your learner sees this panel and pulls back hard to stop the descent. What is the IFH recovery order?
options: Raise the nose, level the wings, then add power
Add full power, raise the nose, then level the wings
Reduce power, level the wings, then raise the nose
Level the wings first, add power, then hold the altitude
quiz.why: For a nose-low attitude with airspeed increasing: reduce power, correct the bank with coordinated aileron and rudder by the turn coordinator, then raise the nose; the instinctive reaction is to pull [[23:189|IFH 7-28]]. Pulling in a spiral tightens it [[34:185|AIM 8-1-5]].

quiz.q: Which safety consideration does the IFH state for the spatial disorientation demonstrations?
options: Only in actual IMC, so the learner feels the real cues of cloud flying
Not at low altitudes, and only with an instructor or safety pilot
Only with the learner's eyes open under the hood
Only at night, when a false horizon is easy to find
quiz.why: A pilot should not attempt these maneuvers at low altitudes or without an instructor pilot or appropriate safety pilot [[23:75|IFH 3-8]]. The demonstrations are flown with the eyes closed or the gaze lowered, not in actual IMC [[23:75|IFH 3-8]].

quiz.q: Your student finished a beer 9 hours before a lesson, feels hung over, and says the 8-hour rule is met. What do you tell her?
options: A hangover still means under the influence; not today
She is legal and fit, since more than 8 hours have passed
She may fly if coffee and water clear the hangover first
She may fly IFR but not VFR, since the autopilot helps
quiz.why: While experiencing a hangover, a pilot is still under the influence of alcohol [[1:437|PHAK 17-15]], and 91.17(a) also bars flying while under the influence, not only within 8 hours [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17(a)]]. There is no way to speed up the destruction of alcohol or relieve a hangover [[34:181|AIM 8-1-1]].

final_quiz.q: Climbing on a winter night with the heater on, you and your learner both get a headache and feel drowsy. What do you do first?
options: Turn the heater up so you both stay awake and alert
Descend to a lower altitude to treat altitude hypoxia
Continue, and see a doctor tomorrow if needed
Shut off the heater and open the fresh air vents
final_quiz.why: Headache or drowsiness with the heater on means suspect CO: shut off the heater and open air vents, use oxygen if available, and seek treatment if symptoms are severe or continue after landing [[34:184|AIM 8-1-4]] [[1:434|PHAK 17-12]]. The AIM says to shut off the heater and open the air vents immediately.

final_quiz.q: A learner had CO symptoms on yesterday's flight and feels better today. Per the PHAK, how long can the body take to get rid of CO?
options: About 30 minutes
Up to 48 hours
About 3 hours
Up to 8 hours
final_quiz.why: CO attaches to hemoglobin about 200 times more easily than oxygen, and the body requires up to 48 hours to dispose of it [[1:434|PHAK 17-12]]. About 3 hours is the PHAK figure for clearing one drink [[1:437|PHAK 17-15]].

final_quiz.q: Why does the PHAK say smoking matters to a pilot even at sea level?
options: It raises blood CO to effects like flying at 8,000 feet
It lowers blood alcohol so a pilot may fly sooner after drinking
It sharpens night vision by keeping the pilot alert
It matters only above 12,500 feet
final_quiz.why: Smoking at sea level can raise the CO concentration in the blood and cause effects similar to flying at 8,000 feet [[1:434|PHAK 17-12]]. Nicotine impairs night vision rather than helping it [[1:439|PHAK 17-17]].

final_quiz.q: Which sign of acute fatigue does the AIH say others notice before the learner does?
options: Blue color in the lips and fingernails
A sudden craving for sugary food
Neglect of secondary tasks
Ringing and buzzing in the ears
final_quiz.why: Inattention, distractibility, errors in timing, neglect of secondary tasks, loss of accuracy and control, lack of awareness of error accumulation and irritability are apparent to others before the individual notices [[25:46|AIH 2-13]] [[25:47|AIH 2-14]]. Blue lips and fingernails are cyanosis, a hypoxia sign [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]].

final_quiz.q: Per the AIH, when is a tired pilot's guard likely to be lowest on a night IFR trip?
options: During preflight, before departure adrenaline
On the takeoff roll and climb into the dark
In the first half hour of cruise on autopilot
At the night approach in weather
final_quiz.why: Late night, fatigue and sustained flight above 5,000 feet can make pilots less critical, and the guard is down most just as the critical part approaches, such as a night instrument approach in weather after a 4-hour flight [[25:21|AIH 1-17]]. Sleep-deprived pilots may not notice sleepiness during preflight and departure [[25:18|AIH 1-14]].

final_quiz.q: Which list does the IFH give as likely to increase susceptibility to spatial disorientation?
options: Illness, medication, alcohol, fatigue, sleep loss, mild hypoxia
Bright sunlight, cold weather and high-wing airplanes
Glass cockpits, autopilots and moving map displays
Sunglasses, headsets and tight shoulder harnesses
final_quiz.why: The IFH coping list says illness, medication, alcohol, fatigue, sleep loss and mild hypoxia are likely to increase susceptibility to spatial disorientation [[23:75|IFH 3-8]] [[23:76|IFH 3-9]].

final_quiz.q: Busy reprogramming the GPS in cloud, your learner lets the airplane roll into a descending turn and does not notice until you point to the altimeter. Which AFH category fits?
options: Somatogravic illusion
Unrecognized spatial disorientation
Recognized spatial disorientation
Incapacitating spatial disorientation
final_quiz.why: Unrecognized spatial disorientation is when the pilot is unaware that an upset is developing and takes no corrective action; many upsets happen while the pilot is engaged in a task that takes attention from the instruments [[24:108|AFH 5-3]]. Recognized means the pilot sees it and corrects it.

final_quiz.q: Flying on top at night over a sloping cloud deck, your learner keeps the wings parallel to the cloud tops. What is it, and what is the fix?
options: Autokinesis; pick one star and stare at it to hold the wings level
Elevator illusion; push the nose down until it lines up with the tops
False horizon; level the wings on the attitude indicator
The leans; tilt the head toward the low wing
final_quiz.why: A sloping cloud formation can give a false horizon, and the pilot may place the airplane in a dangerous attitude [[23:74|IFH 3-7]]. The counter is to disregard the false cue and rely on the flight instruments [[23:70|IFH 3-3]]. Staring at a light at night causes autokinesis [[23:74|IFH 3-7]].

final_quiz.q: Flying into a shallow fog layer near the end of an approach, your learner suddenly steepens the descent. Which illusion explains it?
options: Fog makes the runway look farther away
Fog creates an illusion of banking
Fog makes the airplane seem to slow
Fog gives an illusion of pitching up
final_quiz.why: Penetration of fog can create an illusion of pitching up, and the pilot who does not recognize it steepens the approach, often quite abruptly [[34:186|AIM 8-1-5]].

final_quiz.q: In the IFH's learner-flown disorientation demonstration, what does the learner do?
options: Closes the eyes, tilts the head and follows your control inputs
Flies a full stall with eyes closed while you call airspeed
Flies partial panel with the attitude indicator covered
Enters a spin under the hood until you call for recovery
final_quiz.why: The pilot closes the eyes and tilts the head, the instructor says what control inputs to make, and after a short time the instructor tells the pilot to look up and recover [[23:75|IFH 3-8]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner was prescribed a sedating medicine to be taken every 6 hours. Using the PHAK rule of thumb, how long after the last dose should she wait before flying?
options: At least 6 hours
At least 30 hours
At least 12 hours
At least 2 full days
final_quiz.why: Wait at least five maximal dosing intervals after a medication with potentially adverse side effects: 5 x 6 = 30 hours [[1:440|PHAK 17-18]]. The 48-hour wait is a different rule, for the first dose of any new medicine [[1:440|PHAK 17-18]].

final_quiz.q: Your student says recreational marijuana is legal in your state, so weekend use is fine before Monday's lesson. What has the FAA stated?
options: It is allowed if 8 hours pass, as with alcohol
It is allowed where state law permits it
Its use by airmen is prohibited
It is allowed with an AME's written approval
final_quiz.why: The FAA has stated that marijuana is an illicit drug per federal law and its use by airmen is prohibited, whatever the states allow [[1:439|PHAK 17-17]].

final_quiz.q: A passenger on your learner's IFR trip appears drunk. What does 14 CFR 91.17(b) say?
options: The rule covers crew only, not passengers
The passenger may go if seated in the back
The passenger may go if the flight is short
Except in an emergency, the pilot may not carry the person
final_quiz.why: Except in an emergency, no pilot may allow a person who appears intoxicated to be carried, except a medical patient under proper care [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17(b)]].

final_quiz.q: Midway through unusual attitude practice under the hood, your learner turns pale and sweaty. What does the AIH recommend?
options: End the flight as soon as early sickness appears
Add maneuvers so he builds resistance faster
Have him close his eyes and rest while you fly
Continue but avoid talking until he feels better
final_quiz.why: An instructional flight should be terminated as soon as incipient sickness is experienced, and learners are much less apt to get sick while operating the controls themselves, so resting with his eyes closed while you fly is not the AIH remedy [[25:46|AIH 2-13]].

final_quiz.q: Descending for an approach, your learner gets sharp pain above the eyebrows. What may reduce it, and what afterward?
options: A faster descent, to get through it quickly
A slower descent; a physician if it does not clear
A nasal spray in flight, which reliably works
Holding the breath until the pain stops
final_quiz.why: This is a frontal sinus block, most frequent during descent; slow descent rates can reduce the pain [[1:427|PHAK 17-5]], and if it does not clear shortly after landing a physician should be consulted [[34:184|AIM 8-1-2]]. Sprays usually do not give adequate protection [[34:183|AIM 8-1-2]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner, in the middle of a divorce, insists on finishing an IFR cross-country to keep on schedule as the weather worsens. What does the AIM say about stress like this?
options: It sharpens alertness, so a demanding flight is ideal
It affects VFR pilots, not instrument-rated ones
It can lead to unwarranted risks; consider delaying
It is a grounding condition listed in the regulations
final_quiz.why: Distraction from stress can interfere with judgment so that unwarranted risks are taken, such as flying into deteriorating weather to keep on schedule; when difficulties are greater than usual, consider delaying the flight [[34:181|AIM 8-1-1]]. Stress is not among the regulatory grounding conditions [[25:12|AIH 1-8]], which is why self-assessment matters.

takeaways: For every factor, answer in three parts: the effect, the corrective action and the safety consideration.
In IMC the inner ear and the seat of the pants both lie; the eyes on the instruments are the only reliable sense.
Every vestibular illusion makes the wrong control input feel right: leans, Coriolis, graveyard spiral, somatogravic, inversion, elevator.
Head still in turns, small smooth corrections, ball centered, and in a spiral: reduce power, wings level, then pitch.
Demonstrate disorientation high, with a briefed exchange of controls and you as lookout; start gentle and stop at the first sign of sickness.
Legal at 8 hours is not ready for cloud: alcohol can disturb the inner ear for up to 48 hours.
Heater on plus headache or drowsiness means CO until proven otherwise.
Fatigue shows to you before it shows to the learner and peaks at the night approach; run the same checks on yourself.
cfi_notes: Time of useful consciousness at 20,000 feet: PHAK Figure 17-1 gives 30 minutes or more [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]], while the AIM says the ability to take corrective action is lost in 5 to 12 minutes at 20,000 feet [[34:182|AIM 8-1-2]]. Teach the AIM numbers and say the sources differ.

The PHAK says hypoxia symptoms can be different for each individual [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]]; the AIM says they do not vary in an individual [[34:183|AIM 8-1-2]]. Both fit: they differ between people and repeat in one person, which is why chamber training works.

On nasal sprays the PHAK says drops or sprays may reduce the risk of an ear block with minor congestion, after checking with an AME [[1:427|PHAK 17-5]]; the AIM says sprays and drops usually do not give adequate protection [[34:183|AIM 8-1-2]]. For IFR training with many descents, teach the AIM.

Alcohol timing differs by source: 8 hours and 0.04 in the rule [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17(a)]], about 3 hours per drink and possibly over 16 hours for large amounts in the PHAK [[1:437|PHAK 17-15]], 12 to 24 hours in the AIM [[34:181|AIM 8-1-1]], and inner-ear disturbance up to 48 hours in PHAK Figure 17-9 [[1:439|PHAK 17-17]]. Teach the rule as the floor and the 48 hours as the reason an instrument pilot leaves more margin.

The PHAK writes the limit as blood alcohol less than .04 percent [[1:437|PHAK 17-15]]; 91.17 says an alcohol concentration of 0.04 or greater in blood or breath and defines the units [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17(a)]]. Quote the CFR wording on the checkride.

The sources tie the somatogravic illusion to takeoff [[23:73|IFH 3-6]]. Linking it to the full-power missed approach in cloud is this lesson's application, and it is a good scenario for an examiner who asks how you teach it.

The IFH and PHAK demonstrations are written for the eyes closed or the gaze lowered [[23:75|IFH 3-8]], and the AFH warns that eyes-closed training removes surprise [[24:107|AFH 5-2]]. Tell the examiner what the demonstration can and cannot show, and how you add realistic distractions in later scenario training [[24:108|AFH 5-3]].

If you already hold an airplane CFI, the PTS table for adding the instrument instructor rating lists Area II Tasks A and C, so expect this Task mostly on an initial CFII test. The PTS Introduction still tells evaluators to emphasize your ability to teach spatial disorientation (FAA-S-8081-9E), and the AIH lists spatial disorientation among common PTS special emphasis items [[25:164|AIH 8-6]].
gaps: No source gives a minimum altitude for the disorientation demonstrations; the IFH and PHAK only say not at low altitudes [[23:75|IFH 3-8]] [[1:431|PHAK 17-9]]. Use your school's SOP and the POH.
No source describes flying the demonstrations with a view-limiting device on; they are written for eyes closed or gaze lowered to the floor [[23:75|IFH 3-8]].
No source gives a waiting time to fly after a CO exposure; the PHAK says only that the body needs up to 48 hours to dispose of CO [[1:434|PHAK 17-12]]. Ask an AME.
There is no list of acceptable medications here; the regulations include no specific references to medication usage [[1:438|PHAK 17-16]]. Ask an AME.
How the cabin heater works, whether a CO detector is installed and what oxygen equipment is aboard come from your airplane's POH/AFM and equipment list, not the handbooks.
No source says when a learner may resume after hyperventilation or airsickness on the same day; the AIH says only to end the flight at the first sign of airsickness [[25:46|AIH 2-13]].

activities.title: Which type of hypoxia?
activities.intro: Tap each cause, then tap the type of hypoxia it produces.

items.t: CO from exhaust leaking into the heater air
Donating blood a few days before the flight
Cold cutting circulation to the hands and feet

activities.why: Types and causes from [[1:425|PHAK 17-3]] and [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]]. CO is the most common form of hypemic hypoxia, and one ounce of alcohol can equal about 2,000 feet of extra physiological altitude.

activities.title: True or false: altitude, breathing and trapped gas
activities.intro: Decide whether each statement is true or false.

cards.s: Altitude hypoxia happens because the percentage of oxygen in the air drops as you climb.
cards.why: False. The oxygen concentration stays about 21 percent; altitude hypoxia is due only to the reduced barometric pressure [[34:182|AIM 8-1-2]].

cards.s: A pilot's own hypoxia symptoms tend to repeat, so an altitude chamber flight helps her recognize them later.
cards.why: True. The AIM says symptoms do not vary in an individual, so the chamber experience greatly improves recognition [[34:183|AIM 8-1-2]].

cards.s: In a climb, the pilot has to swallow or yawn to let air out of the middle ear.
cards.why: False. In a climb the expanding air pushes the Eustachian tube open by itself; the descent is when the pilot must open it [[34:183|AIM 8-1-2]].

cards.s: Talking aloud can help a pilot get over hyperventilation.
cards.why: True. Slowing the breathing, breathing into a paper bag or talking aloud helps, and recovery is usually rapid [[1:427|PHAK 17-5]].

cards.s: Fever and anxiety raise the body's oxygen demand, and so its susceptibility to hypoxia.
If decompression sickness symptoms go away during the descent, no medical evaluation is needed.
cards.why: False. Even if the symptoms disappear, land and get a medical evaluation while staying on oxygen; symptoms can also appear after landing [[1:440|PHAK 17-18]].

activities.title: Name the illusion
activities.intro: Tap what the learner feels or does in IMC, then tap the illusion.

pairs.l: After a long, shallow turn in cloud, rolling level feels like banking the other way
Looking down for a chart in a long constant-rate turn brings a sudden feeling of rotation on a different axis
Altitude unwinds in a turn that feels like a wings-level descent, and the pilot pulls back
Full power on a missed approach feels like the nose pitching up
An abrupt level-off from a climb feels like tumbling backward
An updraft in cloud feels like a climb, and the pilot pushes over

activities.why: Illusions from [[34:185|AIM 8-1-5]] and [[23:73|IFH 3-6]]. The missed approach link is an application of the takeoff case the IFH describes.

activities.title: How a graveyard spiral develops
activities.intro: Use the arrows to put the steps in order, first to last, then tap Check.
steps: A prolonged, coordinated, constant-rate turn: the inner-ear fluid catches up and the turn is no longer felt
The airplane loses altitude in the turn unless the pilot makes up for the lost lift
The pilot sees the altitude loss but feels no turn: it seems a wings-level descent
The pilot pulls back on the controls to climb or stop the descent
The spiral tightens and the altitude loss grows, toward loss of control
activities.why: Sequence from [[1:429|PHAK 17-7]] and [[34:185|AIM 8-1-5]]. The way out is reduce power, wings level by the instruments, then raise the nose [[23:189|IFH 7-28]].

activities.title: Read the spiral on the panel
activities.intro: Drag each label to its numbered pin on the nose-low panel.

pins.label: Speed high and rising: reduce power first
Shows the left bank and low nose directly
Unwinding: the cue a disoriented pilot pulls against
Level its miniature airplane with coordinated aileron and rudder
Still turning: proof the airplane is not straight
Shows the descent, along with the altimeter and airspeed

activities.why: Nose-low indications and recovery from [[23:188|IFH 7-27]] and [[23:189|IFH 7-28]]; pulling back against the altitude loss is the graveyard spiral reaction [[34:185|AIM 8-1-5]]. In coordinated flight a turning heading means a bank [[23:168|IFH 7-7]].

activities.title: True or false: alcohol and medicine
activities.intro: Decide whether each statement is true or false.

cards.s: Alcohol can cause inner-ear disturbance and spatial disorientation for up to 48 hours.
cards.why: True. PHAK Figure 17-9 lists it among alcohol's effects [[1:439|PHAK 17-17]].

cards.s: A pilot at 0.04 alcohol concentration 8 hours after drinking may fly, since the time limit is met.
cards.why: False. 91.17(a) bars a crewmember with an alcohol concentration of 0.04 or greater, whatever the time since drinking [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17(a)]].

cards.s: Coffee and a cold shower speed up the destruction of alcohol.
cards.why: False. There is simply no way of increasing the destruction of alcohol or alleviating a hangover [[34:181|AIM 8-1-1]].

cards.s: Any medication that depresses the nervous system can make a pilot more susceptible to hypoxia.
The regulations contain a list of acceptable over-the-counter medications.
cards.why: False. The regulations include no specific references to medication usage; 61.53 and 91.17 are the two to know [[1:438|PHAK 17-16]].

cards.s: After the first dose of a new medicine, wait at least 48 hours before flying.
cards.why: True. This shows whether it has side effects that would make flying unsafe [[1:440|PHAK 17-18]].

activities.title: Work the numbers you will teach
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: Cabin altitude 13,000 feet for 50 minutes. For how many minutes must the required minimum flight crew use oxygen?
items.why: Above 12,500 up to 14,000 feet, oxygen is required for the part of the flight at those altitudes of more than 30 minutes: 50 - 30 = 20 minutes [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211(a)]].

items.q: A medicine with sedating side effects is taken every 8 hours. Using the PHAK rule of five maximal dosing intervals, how many hours should your learner wait after the last dose?
A learner finished a dive with no decompression stops at 1000. The IFR flight will cruise at 10,000 feet MSL. At least how many hours after the dive should departure be?
items.why: Above 8,000 feet, wait at least 24 hours after any dive; the 12-hour wait applies only up to 8,000 feet [[34:184|AIM 8-1-2]].

items.q: With no flight training before 0700, you have given 6.3 hours of flight training since 0700. How many more hours may you give before 0700 tomorrow?
items.why: 8 - 6.3 = 1.7 hours in the 24 consecutive hours [[60:346|14 CFR 61.195(a)]].

activities.title: A night IFR lesson, step by step
activities.intro: You are the CFII on a night instrument lesson. Make each call as it unfolds.

steps.s: 1700. Your instrument student arrives for a night IFR cross-country with two approaches at an unfamiliar airport. She says she slept 5 hours and had a hard week at work.
options: Go as planned, since she needs the night IFR time before her checkride
Fly it, but let her nap in cruise while you fly the airplane
Run IMSAFE with her and move the flight or make it a ground lesson
Cut it to one approach, which takes care of the fatigue risk
steps.why: With acute fatigue, stay on the ground [[1:435|PHAK 17-13]]; stress with fatigue is an extremely hazardous combination [[34:181|AIM 8-1-1]]. Rescheduling is the AIH's remedy for learner aeromedical issues [[25:191|AIH 10-7]].

steps.s: Another night, she is rested. In cloud on vectors, in a long right turn, she ducks her head to find the approach chart on the floor.
options: Let her, since a quick look down is harmless in a standard-rate turn
Tell her to keep her head up, fly the turn by the instruments, and get the chart slowly
Take the controls without a word and let her search for the chart
Have her steepen the turn so the search takes less time
steps.why: A head movement in a prolonged constant-rate turn under IFR can set off the Coriolis illusion [[34:185|AIM 8-1-5]]; retrieve items with minimal head movement [[23:73|IFH 3-6]]. If you take the controls, say so: "I have the flight controls" [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].

steps.s: Level at 7,000 feet with the heater on, she says she has a headache and feels sleepy. You feel a little dizzy too.
options: Suspect CO: heater off, vents open, oxygen if available
Turn the heater up so neither of you gets cold and sleepy
Climb to cooler air at a higher altitude to clear your heads
Continue the lesson and check for symptoms after landing
steps.why: Headache, drowsiness or dizziness with the heater on means suspect CO: heater off, vents open, oxygen if available, and medical treatment if symptoms are severe or continue after landing [[34:184|AIM 8-1-4]] [[1:434|PHAK 17-12]].

steps.s: The air clears. On the missed approach she adds full power in cloud and the nose drifts below the climb attitude; she says the climb felt too steep.
options: Inversion illusion: level off abruptly to stop the sensation
Elevator illusion: reduce power until the feeling stops
No illusion: lower the nose further to build airspeed
Somatogravic illusion: hold the climb attitude on the attitude indicator
steps.why: Rapid acceleration creates the illusion of a nose-up attitude and the disoriented pilot pushes over [[23:73|IFH 3-6]]; trust the instruments and disregard the sensation [[23:76|IFH 3-9]].

steps.s: 2330. Back on the ground, she wants to fly the two approaches again tonight. You have given 7.5 hours of flight training since 0800.
options: Fly one more hour, since the limit resets at midnight
Fly, since the rule limits only the learner's hours
Stop: half an hour is left in your 8 hours, and you are both tired
Fly, and log her as PIC so the time does not count for you
steps.why: A flight instructor may not conduct more than 8 hours of flight training in any 24 consecutive hours [[60:346|14 CFR 61.195(a)]], and a night approach at the end of a long day is when the guard is lowest [[25:21|AIH 1-17]].
